about: The Wang Bi lesson on 8-Bit Oracle's X, two hours after Six Lines posts it (series/social/2026-09-30-wangbi-lesson.json). A native video, not a quote: the user, 2026-09-28: 'yes for 8-Bit Oracle X account, you see what we've been posting. i think for this, we can take a matter of fact tone in terms of how we favor Wang Bi's structural interpretations of the I-Ching as it matches quite well to computing, programs, and logic'. Written in the account's form (long post, one terminal line, then the link), read from its published drafts on 2026-09-28. Sources: Wang Bi's 周易略例 (明彖, 明象, 辯位) and the 四庫全書總目 易類 preface ('王弼盡黜象數，說以老莊'). Checked against chinese-classics-reference on 2026-09-28: the Tang court's subcommentary kept only his commentary (四庫總目, 周易正義: '穎達等奉詔作疏，始專崇王註而衆說皆廢'); nested trigrams, changing hexagrams, the five phases (明象: '互體不足，遂及卦變，變又不足，推致五行') and days and seasons (孫盛 in 三國志 note: '日時歲月，五氣相推，弼皆擯落'); 3 and 5 yang places, 2 and 4 yin, 1 and 6 no fixed kind (辯位); answering pairs are yin and yang (略例下: '凡陰陽者，相求之物也'); died at 24 sui (何劭's biography: '時年二十四'). The first draft's 'until Zhu Xi's replaced it in 1313' is not in the library, so it is dropped.
title: Wang Bi lesson (video, full 3:48), structure as code
alt: A green terminal teaches how Wang Bi read a hexagram: positions, centres, answering lines and the master line, built one part at a time.

platforms.x:
Wang Bi (226–249) died at 23. In the 7th century the Tang court's official subcommentary kept his I-Ching commentary as the only one to teach, and the others fell out of use. His method reads a hexagram as a data structure.

Han scholars read each hexagram through layers of correspondence: trigrams nested inside trigrams, hexagrams changing into others, the five phases, days and seasons. Wang Bi dropped them. His rule, 得意忘象: once you have the meaning, let go of the image.

What he kept is structure. Six lines, each yang or yin, read by position:

Lines 2 to 5 hold rank: 3 and 5 are yang places, 2 and 4 yin places. Lines 1 and 6 are the start and the end, with no fixed kind.
Lines 2 and 5 are the centres of the lower and upper trigram.
1 answers 4, 2 answers 5, 3 answers 6, but only when one is yin and the other yang.
When one line differs from the other five, it rules the hexagram. His phrase: the few rule the many.

An index, a parity check, a pairwise XOR, a count. Anyone can run it on any of the 64 and get the same answer. That is why Six Lines is built on it.

The Qing imperial catalog's line on him: he threw out the image-numbers entirely and explained the text through Laozi and Zhuangzi. We keep the first half.

> popcount(師 Army) == 1 # one yang rules five yin

A 4-minute lesson in reading a hexagram his way, made for @sixlinesapp → sixlines.day
